# Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation

413

Yurui Lai Affiliation: Hong Kong Baptist University, Hong Kong, China
email: <csyrlai@comp.hkbu.edu.hk> , Samir Moustafa Affiliation: CeMM
Research Center for Molecular Medicine of the Austrian Academy of
Sciences  
Universität Vienna, Vienna, Austria email: <samir.moustafa@univie.ac.at>
, Renchi Yang^(†) Affiliation: Hong Kong Baptist University, Hong Kong,
China email: <renchi@hkbu.edu.hk> and Tsz Nam Chan Affiliation: Shenzhen
University, Shenzhen, China email: <edisonchan@szu.edu.cn>

###### Abstract.

Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs) have emerged as an expressive data model
for integrating graph topology with rich textual semantics. Existing
representation learning methods over TAGs suffer from severe scalability
bottlenecks, particularly together with Large Language Models (LLMs).
While data distillation offers a promising data-centric solution,
existing methods fail to capture the complex interplay between graph and
text modalities, struggle with the label scarcity inherent in
semi-supervised settings, and lack the ability to produce the
human-readable textual attributes required for downstream LLM-based
tasks.

To address these challenges, we propose STAD, a unified semi-supervised
framework guided by the Wasserstein Distance (WSD). Grounded in our
empirical findings on real TAGs, STAD introduces a graph-text
collaborative encoding module that utilizes dual-pathway encoders
(graph-aware and -free) within a collaborative self-training scheme to
harvest reliable pseudo-labels and fuse complementary graph-text
features. Furthermore, we develop a theoretically grounded WSD-based
graph sketching algorithm and a cost-effective LLM text synthesis
module, which leverages cluster-based keyword extraction to generate
coherent, human-readable summaries for condensed nodes. Extensive
experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that STAD achieves a
state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-off in terms of both GNN-
and LLM-based downstream tasks, enabling effective and efficient TAG
learning or analytics.

###### Keywords: 

Data Distillation; Text-Attributed Graphs; Semi-Supervised
Classification; Text Synthesis

## 1. Introduction

Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs) have emerged as a popular graph data
paradigm, integrating rich semantic text with complex relations among
textual entities ([Yan et al., 2023](#bib.bib7); [Feng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib11); [Chen et al., 2024b](#bib.bib1); [Zhang et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib16)). By bridging the gap between graph data and natural
language, TAGs unlock the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) for
diverse cross-domain applications ([Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib13); [Liu
et al., 2023](#bib.bib17); [Jin et al., 2024](#bib.bib14); [Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib12)), from drug discovery ([Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib50))
to fraud detection ([Yang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib51)), etc. Through
exploiting the synergy between two modalities in TAGs, recent hybrid
frameworks combining Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) ([Kipf and Welling,
2017](#bib.bib8); [Veličković et al., 2018](#bib.bib9); [Hamilton et
al., 2017](#bib.bib10)) with LLMs have achieved remarkable results for
learning tasks over TAGs ([Zhao et al., 2023](#bib.bib23); [He et al.,
2024](#bib.bib19); [Zhang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib22); [Chen et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib1); [Zhu et al., 2024](#bib.bib18); [Tang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib20); [Chen et al., 2024a](#bib.bib21); [Sun et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24); [Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)). Despite the
advancements made, these approaches still suffer from a critical
scalability bottleneck in practical deployment, as real-world TAGs often
scale to hundreds of thousands of nodes and edges ([Chen et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib1)). The integration with LLMs further significantly
increases the computational and financial overhead demanded by these
methods, which, in turn, severely limits their applicability in
large-scale industrial and scientific scenarios.

Data distillation offers a promising data-centric solution to this
scalability challenge in large-scale learning tasks ([Sachdeva and
McAuley, 2023](#bib.bib25); [Lei and Tao, 2023](#bib.bib26)). Its goal
is to synthesize a condensed, small-scale dataset that preserves the
training dynamics and information of the original large-scale data. In
recent years, substantial efforts ([Jin et al., 2022](#bib.bib28); [Yang
et al., 2023](#bib.bib29); [Liu et al., 2024](#bib.bib31); [Lai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib30)) have been made towards graph distillation (a.k.a.
graph condensation) and text distillation ([Li and Li,
2021](#bib.bib44); [Sucholutsky and Schonlau, 2021](#bib.bib32);
[Maekawa et al., 2023](#bib.bib38); [Tao et al., 2024](#bib.bib45)),
where the former seeks to condense the original graphs with nodal
attributes into small ones, while the latter focuses on compressing text
into concise semantic representations. However, extending these
successes to TAGs still presents unique, non-trivial challenges.
Firstly, the naive combination of graph and text distillation fails to
capture the complex interplay between graph and textual modalities ([Jin
et al., 2022](#bib.bib28); [Zhou et al., 2025](#bib.bib49)). Graph
distillation methods typically treat text as static numerical features,
failing to maintain semantic consistency, while text distillation
overlooks structural features. Second, existing graph condensation
methods simply construct continuous features that lack interpretability
as node attributes. But for TAGs, it is necessary to generate
human-readable textual attributes such that the distilled TAGs remain
compatible with downstream LLM-based tasks, e.g., prompt-based learning
or explanation generation ([He et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)). On top of
that, real-world TAGs often present severe label scarcity, where
standard distillation techniques that often rely on abundant supervision
to align gradients or distributions, falter or even fail.

To overcome the aforementioned challenges, this paper proposes STAD
(Semi-supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation), a unified
framework designed to distill TAGs into compact, human-readable graphs
under semi-supervised settings. Our approach is grounded in our
quantitative empirical studies, where we identify that (i) graph-aware
models (GNNs) and graph-free models (MLPs) capture complementary
information, and simply optimizing one modality is insufficient for
effective condensation of TAGs, and (ii) the Wasserstein Distance
(WSD) ([Solomon et al., 2015a](#bib.bib39); [Yang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib29)) between the distributions of original and condensed
graphs is strongly correlated with downstream performance. Inspired by
these observations, we first propose a graph-text collaborative encoding
module, which employs dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and -free
pathways) within a collaborative self-training scheme as complementary
learners, where pseudo-supervision is iteratively generated for better
feature fusion, thereby mitigating label scarcity and cross-modality
misalignment. Subsequently, building on these fused features, a
theoretically-grounded graph sketching aiming at minimizing the WSD
between distribution shifts between original and condensed TAGs is
leveraged for condensing both graph topology, attributes, and labels.
Furthermore, we construct textual attributes for distilled graphs
through our Keywords-based LLM text synthesis. Instead of optimizing
abstract embeddings or directly harnessing LLMs for text summarization,
which is powerful but costly  ([Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib37); [Zhang
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib34)), STAD resorts to a three-stage pipeline,
where keywords are first extracted from condensed clusters, and LLMs are
then cost-effectively harnessed to generate coherent candidate text from
these keywords. Lastly, a WSD-validation-guided selection strategy is
adopted to identify the synthetic texts that best preserve the
distributional characteristics of the original data.

In sum, our major contributions in this paper are as follows:

- •
  We pioneer the systematic exploration of TAG distillation. We propose
  the use of WSD as a reliable metric to quantify distribution shifts in
  TAGs, offering a theoretical basis for assessing distillation quality
  in graph-text contexts.
- •
  We develop STAD framework, which integrates graph-text collaborative
  encoding to resolve label scarcity and modality misalignment and
  modality fusion, and WSD-guided graph sketching and keywords-based LLM
  text synthesis to create high-quality condensed graphs and textual
  attributes.
- •
  Our extensive experiments on multiple benchmark TAG datasets
  demonstrate that STAD consistently achieves a state-of-the-art
  performance-compression trade-off in both GNN- and LLM-based node
  classification tasks, compared to existing graph or text distillation
  solutions.

## 2. Related Work

Graph Distillation. Graph Distillation (or Graph Condensation) is a
data-centric solution to reduce the computational and storage costs of
GNNs on large-scale graphs, whose goal is to synthesize compact graphs,
maintaining the key information of original graphs for competitive model
performance. GCond ([Jin et al., 2022](#bib.bib28)) is a simple
gradient-matching based method which synthesizes graphs by matching the
GNN’s gradients on the synthesis and original graphs. SGDD ([Yang et
al., 2023](#bib.bib29)) proposes a structure-broadcasting scheme to
preserve the original structural information in the gradient matching
process. GCDM ([Liu et al., 2022](#bib.bib40)) and GDEM ([Liu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib31)) are distribution matching-based methods, with GCDM
aligning the receptive field distributions of synthetic and original
graphs via MMD, and GDEM focusing on matching the eigenbasis and
spectral distributions of the two graphs. SFGC ([Zheng et al.,
2023](#bib.bib41)) and GCSR ([Liu et al., 2024](#bib.bib31)) are
trajectory matching-based distillation methods, which align the
long-term learning dynamics of GNNs on synthetic and original graphs.
CGC ([Gao et al., 2025](#bib.bib43)) and ClustGDD ([Lai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib30)) are clustering-based methods, with CGC conducting
class partition to derive condensed node features and topology in closed
form, and ClustGDD optimizes FID between synthetic and original graphs
via clustering.

Text Distillation. Text distillation is the process of synthesizing
compact text datasets for NLP tasks. TDD ([Sucholutsky and Schonlau,
2021](#bib.bib32)) updates network parameters via gradient descent with
distilled samples and soft labels, computes loss on real text, and
optimizes the distilled component by loss gradients to capture text
semantics, then decodes distilled text using the original word embedding
dictionary. DD4TC ([Li and Li, 2021](#bib.bib44)) uses the gradients
from training on the original texts to be back-propagated to the
distillation texts. ASD ([Maekawa et al., 2023](#bib.bib38))
simultaneously optimizes distilled input embeddings, soft labels, and
attention labels using gradient descent, and guides model parameter
updates by combining task loss and transformer attention loss.
DiLM ([Maekawa et al., 2025](#bib.bib46)) uses a GPT-2 model to generate
candidate distilled texts, and learn a generation probability via
matching the learner’s gradients on both original and distilled texts.
DaLLME ([Tao et al., 2024](#bib.bib45)) conducts k-centroid on text
embeddings and translates the clustered embedding center back to
readable text via a T5 ([Raffel et al., 2020](#bib.bib47)) model
finetuned on embedding-text pairs constructed from the original dataset.

Although many distillation methods exist for graph and text, no
dedicated scheme has been designed for TAGs. Single-modal distillation
cannot fully exploit the other modality, motivating us to propose a
collaborative graph-text distillation scheme for TAGs.

TAG Representation Learning. LMs (including LLMs), combined with
traditional GNNs, have leveraged their abilities on TAG representation
learning based on rich semantic information of raw texts in TAGs. LMs
can serve as TAG encoders by integrating graph topology and texts into
the embedding space ([Yan et al., 2023](#bib.bib7); [Chen et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib1); [Zhu et al., 2024](#bib.bib18)). ENGINE ([Zhu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib18)) combines the inter-layer embeddings of LLMs for text
encoding. LMs can serve as TAG augmenters, e.g., TAPE ([He et al.,
2024](#bib.bib19)) makes LLMs to directly generate predictions and
explanations to enrich the text of nodes. CTGL ([Zhou et al.,
2025](#bib.bib49)) quantitatively compares the complementarity between
graph structure and textual attributes, serially augments and encodes
TAG using GNNs and LMs, and fuses graph structure and text in a
contrastive way. LMs can be the predictors to give final predictions of
TAG learning tasks ([Tang et al., 2024](#bib.bib20); [Chen et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib21)). LLaGA ([Chen et al., 2024a](#bib.bib21)) puts the
serialized graph structure and node texts into an LLM to generate
predictions and natural language descriptions. ([Wu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15)) gives an extensive survey of different types of LLMs’
performance on TAG node classification. However, these methods will
suffer from training efficiency problems when the TAGs scale up, which
motivates the exploration of TAG distillation. We In this work, we
define LLM4TAG as large language models tailored for TAG learning
tasks ([Su et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)), and use this standardized
terminology consistently in the experimental section.

## 3. Preliminaries

### 3.1. Notations and Problem Formulation

Notations. Let $`\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathcal{S})`$ be
a Text-Attributed Graph (TAG), where $`\mathcal{V}`$ denotes the set of
$`N`$ nodes ($`N=|\mathcal{V}|`$), $`\mathcal{E}`$ denotes the set of
$`M`$ edges ($`M=|\mathcal{E}|`$),
$`\mathcal{S}=\{s_{i}\}_{v_{i}\in\mathcal{V}}`$ is the collection of
text sequences for nodes. We denote the neighbor set of $`v_{i}`$ as
$`\mathcal{N}(v_{i})`$ with degree $`d(v_{i})=|\mathcal{N}(v_{i})|`$.
$`\mathbf{A}\in\{0,1\}^{N\times N}`$ is used to represent the adjacency
matrix of $`\mathcal{G}`$ (where $`\mathbf{A}_{i,j}=1`$ if
$`(v_{i},v_{j})\in\mathcal{E}`$, otherwise $`\mathbf{A}_{i,j}=0`$) and
$`\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}`$ symbolizes the diagonal degree
matrix. The normalized adjacency matrix is
$`\tilde{\mathbf{A}}=\mathbf{D}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-\frac{1}{2}}`$.
Let $`\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}`$ be the text embeddings of
nodes, wherein $`\mathbf{X}_{i}`$ (the $`i`$-th row) denotes the
vectorized encoding of $`s_{i}`$ for node $`v_{i}\in\mathcal{V}`$ via a
text encoder $`g:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbf{X}`$. By default, we adopt a
pretrained Sentence-BERT (SBERT) ([Reimers and Gurevych,
2019](#bib.bib27)) as $`g`$ throughout this paper. Let $`\mathcal{Y}`$
be the task-specific class set, and $`K=|\mathcal{Y}|`$ is the number of
node classes. We denote by $`\mathbf{Y}\in\{0,1\}^{N\times K}`$ the
ground-truth label matrix of $`\mathcal{G}`$ where
$`\mathbf{Y}_{i,k}=1`$ if $`y_{k}\in\mathcal{Y}`$ ($`1\leq k\leq K`$) is
$`v_{i}`$’s ground-truth class label and $`0`$ otherwise. Under
semi-supervised settings, only a small set of nodes
$`\mathcal{V}_{\text{tr}}\subseteq\mathcal{V}`$
($`|\mathcal{V}_{\text{tr}}|\ll N`$) are labeled, referred to as
training samples.

Problem Formulation. The overarching goal of Text-Attributed Graph
Distillation (TAGD) is to distill a compact, high-fidelity compressed
TAG
$`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}=(\mathcal{V}^{\prime},\mathcal{E}^{\prime},\mathcal{S}^{\prime})`$
from the original larger $`\mathcal{G}`$, where $`\mathcal{V}^{\prime}`$
($`N^{\prime}=|\mathcal{V}^{\prime}|\ll N`$) and
$`\mathcal{E}^{\prime}`$ ($`M^{\prime}=|\mathcal{E}^{\prime}|\ll M`$)
stand for the node and edge sets of $`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$,
respectively, and
$`\mathcal{S}^{\prime}=\{s^{\prime}_{i}\}_{v^{\prime}_{i}\in\mathcal{V}^{\prime}}`$
represents human-readable text sequences for condensed nodes therein.
Let $`\mathbf{A}^{\prime}`$ and $`\mathbf{Y}^{\prime}`$ be the adjacency
matrix and node labels of $`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$, respectively.
Formally, the objective of the TAGD problem can be formulated as:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (1) |     |

````math
\begin{gathered}\min_{\mathcal{G}^{\prime}}\,{f}\left(\mathcal{M}_{\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\mathcal{G}^{\prime}}}(\mathbf{A},\mathcal{S}),\mathbf{Y}\right)\\
\text{s.t.}\,\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\mathcal{G}^{\prime}}=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}f\left(\mathcal{M}_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\mathbf{A}^{\prime},\mathcal{S}^{\prime}),\mathbf{Y}^{\prime}\right),\\
\end{gathered}
``` |  |

where $`\mathcal{M}_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}`$ denotes a general model
parameterized by $`\boldsymbol{\phi}`$, and $`f(\cdot)`$ is the
task-specific criteria. In this paper, we consider the semi-supervised
node classification setting and the distillation ratio is defined as
$`r=\frac{N^{\prime}}{|\mathcal{V}_{\text{tr}}|}\leq 1`$.

### 3.2. 2-Wasserstein Distance (WSD)

The 2-Wasserstein Distance (WSD) in optimal transport ([Solomon et al.,
2015b](#bib.bib42)) is a classic distance function used to measure shift
between two probability distributions $`\mathcal{P}`$ and
$`\mathcal{Q}`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\textsf{WSD}(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q})=\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q})}\int_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}}\|\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{q}\|\,\text{d}\gamma(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})
``` |  |

where $`\Gamma(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q})`$ is the set of joint
distributions with marginals $`\mathcal{P}`$ and $`\mathcal{Q}`$,
$`\mathcal{X}`$ is the feature space, and $`\|\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{q}\|`$
is the Euclidean distance. SGDD ([Yang et al., 2023](#bib.bib29)) uses
WSD as an alternative to the Laplacian Energy Distribution shift
coefficient for graph structure optimization. ClustGDD ([Lai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib30)) finds a correlation between Fréchet Inception
Distance (FID) and accuracy of GNNs on original and synthetic graphs,
where FID between two multivariate Gaussian distributions
$`N(\mu_{\mathcal{P}},\Sigma_{\mathcal{P}})`$ and
$`N(\mu_{\mathcal{Q}},\Sigma_{\mathcal{Q}})`$, given by

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{FID}(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q})=\|\mu_{\mathcal{P}}-\mu_{\mathcal{Q}}\|_{2}^{2}+\operatorname{Tr}\big(\Sigma_{\mathcal{P}}+\Sigma_{\mathcal{Q}}-2(\Sigma_{\mathcal{P}}\Sigma_{\mathcal{Q}})^{1/2}\big),
``` |  |

corresponds to a special case of WSD when the underlying distributions
are multivariate Gaussians. Next, we will compute WSD between original
and synthetic textual attributes, graph structures under various
distillation ratios, and comprehensively investigate the correlations
between WSD and the model performance.

Figure 2. WSD and node classification accuracy on condensed TAGs vs.
distillation ratio.

### 3.3. Preliminary Studies

We empirically investigate the TAGD task over four real datasets (Cora,
Photo, History, and WikiCS) pertaining to two aspects before entering
into the algorithmic design of our proposed STAD.

Graph-Aware vs. Graph-Free. Since both graph structures and textual
attributes encode rich semantics in TAGs, a natural question is their
roles in the downstream task, i.e., semi-supervised node classification.
To this end, we compare the graph-aware (GA) model, i.e., GNNs using
$`\mathbf{X}`$ and $`\mathbf{A}`$ for node classification, against the
graph-free (GF) model, i.e., MLPs using pure text attribute of
$`\mathcal{S}`$. Let $`\mathcal{C}_{\text{GA}}`$ and
$`\mathcal{C}_{\text{GF}}`$ be the sets of node samples whose labels are
correctly predicted by the GA and GF models, respectively. Accordingly,
$`\overline{\mathcal{C}_{\text{GA}}\cup\mathcal{C}_{\text{GF}}}`$ stands
for the complementary set containing node samples whose labels cannot be
correctly predicted by both models.

Fig. [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3.2. 2-Wasserstein Distance (WSD) ‣ 3. Preliminaries ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
reports the proportions of different sets on the four tested datasets.
It can be observed that although $`\mathcal{C}_{\text{GA}}`$ and
$`\mathcal{C}_{\text{GF}}`$ have a big overlap ($`43.9\%`$-$`64.4\%`$),
their differences are still considerable. Firstly, this observation
underscores the indispensability of both structural and textual
information and their complementary strengths in TAGs. Additionally, the
$`\mathcal{C}_{\text{GF}}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{\text{GA}}`$ part implies
that using GNNs with $`\mathbf{X}`$ in the GA model fails to fully
capture the textual semantics in $`\mathcal{S}`$, necessitating new
feature encoders.

Relation between the WSD and Accuracy. Next, we empirically analyze the
distributional shifts between attribute matrices of the original TAG
$`\mathcal{G}`$ and the condensed TAG $`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$, their
topological structures (i.e., adjacency matrices), their fused
representations via GNNs, as well as their relations to node
classification performance.
Fig. [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2. 2-Wasserstein Distance (WSD) ‣ 3. Preliminaries ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
displays the WSD values between $`\mathbf{X}`$ and
$`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}`$, $`\mathbf{A}`$ and $`{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime}`$,
$`\textsf{GNN}(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{X})`$ and
$`\textsf{GNN}({\mathbf{A}}^{\prime},\mathbf{X}^{\prime})`$, and node
classification accuracies (Acc) when varying the distillation ratios,
i.e., $`r\in[0.05,0.25,0.5,1.0]`$ on the four real datasets (Cora,
Photo, History, and WikiCS).

The empirical results reveal a key trend.
$`\textsf{WSD}({\mathbf{X}},{\mathbf{X}}^{\prime})`$,
$`\textsf{WSD}({\mathbf{A}},{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime})`$, and
$`\textsf{WSD}(\textsf{GNN}(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{X}),\textsf{GNN}({\mathbf{A}}^{\prime},\mathbf{X}^{\prime}))`$,
increase constantly as $`r`$ is decreased (i.e., their distributional
shifts enlarge), while the classification performance keeps going down.
This observation suggests that maximizing the node classification
performance over the TAG $`\mathcal{G}`$ in
Eq. ([1](#S3.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 3.1. Notations and Problem Formulation ‣ 3. Preliminaries ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation"))
can be equivalently transformed into the problem of reducing the
discrepancy between $`\mathcal{G}`$ and $`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$ in
terms of both graph structures and attributes, e.g., minimizing
$`\textsf{WSD}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{X}^{\prime})`$ and
$`\textsf{WSD}(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{A}^{\prime})`$ jointly. To reduce
bias, we compute the mean and std of the results from different baseline
distillation methods.

## 4. Methodology

This section presents our STAD method for TAGD under semi-supervised
settings. As illustrated in
Fig. [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1. Graph-Text Collaborative Encoding ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation"),
STAD includes three key modules for feature encoding in TAGs, graph
sketching, and synthesis of textual attributes. We begin with
elucidating our graph-text collaborative encoding model for generating
node feature vectors $`\mathbf{H}`$ in
§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1. Graph-Text Collaborative Encoding ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation"),
followed by constructing the sketching matrix $`\mathbf{S}`$ for graph
condensation in
§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2. WSD-based Graph Sketching ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation").
§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3. Keywords-based Text Synthesis with LLMs ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
delineates our cost-effective approach for synthesizing textual
attributes of nodes in $`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$ with LLMs. For the
interest of space, we defer the complete algorithm and provide the cost
analysis to
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Complete Algorithm and Analysis ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation").

### 4.1. Graph-Text Collaborative Encoding

As per our analysis in
§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3. Preliminary Studies ‣ 3. Preliminaries ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation"),
we propose to adopt dual-pathway encoders and leverage collaborative
self-training to unearth the complementary information underlying the
graph and text features for enhanced feature encoding.

Dual-Pathway Encoders. Since the GNN encoder will lose distinct features
underlying $`\mathcal{S}`$, as revealed in
§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3. Preliminary Studies ‣ 3. Preliminaries ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation"),
STAD includes two paths of encoders: a GA (or graph) encoder via GCNs,
and a GF (or text) encoder via an MLP layer. Specifically,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (2) |  |
``` math
\mathbf{H}^{\text{\tiny GA}}=\textsf{GCN}(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{X}),\ \mathbf{H}^{\text{\tiny GF}}=\textsf{MLP}(\mathbf{X}),
``` |  |

whose $`i`$-th rows
$`\mathbf{H}_{i}^{\text{\tiny GA}}\in\mathbb{R}^{h}`$ and
$`\mathbf{H}_{i}^{\text{\tiny GF}}\in\mathbb{R}^{h}`$ signify the
feature vectors of node $`v_{i}`$ output by the dual-pathway encoders.
Subsequently, STAD calculates attention weights by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (3) |  |
``` math
\alpha^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i}=\sigma\left(\mathbf{W}_{\text{att}}\cdot\mathbf{H}_{i}^{\text{\tiny GA}}+\mathbf{b}_{\text{att}}\right),\ \alpha^{\text{\tiny GF}}_{i}=1-\alpha^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i},
``` |  |

where $`\mathbf{W}_{\text{att}}\in\mathbb{R}^{h}`$ and
$`\mathbf{b}_{\text{att}}\in\mathbb{R}`$ are learnable parameters, and
$`\sigma(\cdot)`$ denotes the sigmoid function. Accordingly, the fused
predicted label distributions (or soft labels) of each node $`v_{i}`$
can be derived via a weighted element-wise summation ($`\odot`$ is the
element-wise multiplication) of the feature vectors from both encoders:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (4) |  |
``` math
\mathbf{P}_{i}=\textsf{softmax}(\alpha^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i}\odot\mathbf{H}_{i}^{\text{\tiny GA}}+\alpha^{\text{\tiny GF}}_{i}\odot\mathbf{H}_{i}^{\text{\tiny GF}}).
``` |  |

Inspired by the adaptive mechanism in ([Bo et al., 2021](#bib.bib5);
[Luan et al., 2022](#bib.bib4)), STAD learns attention weights to
automatically fuse graph and text features. In particular, the soft
labels derived from the GA and GF encoders can be represented as
follows:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i}=\textsf{softmax}(\mathbf{H}_{i}^{\text{\tiny GA}}),\ \mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GF}}_{i}=\textsf{softmax}(\mathbf{H}_{i}^{\text{\tiny GF}}).
``` |  |

![Refer to caption](2607.20477v1/STAD_final.png)

Figure 3. The Overview of STAD

Collaborative Self-Training. To fully leverage scarce labeled data, we
introduce collaborative self-training (CoST) that treats GA and GF
encoders as complementary learners, as they capture distinct features
predictive of different labels. Let $`\hat{\mathbf{Y}}`$ be the label
matrix consisting of both true labels and hard pseudo-labels obtained
based on label distribution $`\mathbf{P}`$, and
$`\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\text{\tiny GA}}`$ and
$`\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\text{\tiny GF}}`$ are counterparts from
$`\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}}`$ and $`\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GF}}`$,
respectively. CoST trains the model with such predictions and
pseudo-labels by jointly optimizing the following composite loss:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| (5) |  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\textsf{CE}(\mathbf{P},\hat{\mathbf{Y}})+\textsf{CE}(\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GF}},\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\text{\tiny GF}})+\textsf{CE}(\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}},\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\text{\tiny GA}}),`$ |  |

where $`\textsf{CE}(\cdot,\cdot)`$ denotes the cross-entropy loss.

Next, we elaborate on the constructions of $`\hat{\mathbf{Y}}`$,
$`\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\text{\tiny GA}}`$, and
$`\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\text{\tiny GF}}`$. Unlike conventional
self-training ([Lee and others, 2013](#bib.bib53); [Li et al.,
2018](#bib.bib54)), where the pseudo-labels from a single model are
prone to error accumulation, CoST employs a consensus verification
between GA and GF modules to filter uncertain pseudo-labels. For ease of
exposition, we represent by $`\mathcal{U}`$,
$`\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GA}}`$, and $`\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GF}}`$
the labeled node sets of $`\hat{\mathbf{Y}}`$,
$`\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\text{\tiny GA}}`$, and
$`\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\text{\tiny GF}}`$, respectively. Initially,
$`\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GA}}=\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GF}}=\mathcal{V}_{\text{tr}}`$.
We iteratively expand these labeled node sets by identifying
pseudo-labeled data from $`\mathcal{V}\setminus\mathcal{U}`$.

Specifically, in each epoch, we obtain a set $`\mathcal{R}`$ of
candidate nodes for pseudo-labeling based on the GA pathway
$`\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}}`$ by selecting the $`\rho`$ proportion of
unlabeled nodes with the highest confidence scores where the confidence
score of $`v_{i}`$ is denoted by
$`\max_{1\leq k\leq K}\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i,k}`$. Notice that
the value of $`\rho`$ is incremented by 0.1 per epoch until reaching a
maximum of 1.0 as in ([Karisani, 2023](#bib.bib36)). Subsequently, the
candidate set $`\mathcal{R}`$ is partitioned into a consensus set
$`\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny CS}}`$ and a disagreement set
$`\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}`$ by the predictions in the GF pathway
$`\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GF}}`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny CS}}=\{v_{i}\in\mathcal{R}|y^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i}=y^{\text{\tiny GF}}_{i}\},\ \mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}=\{v_{i}\in\mathcal{R}|y^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i}\neq y^{\text{\tiny GF}}_{i}\}=\mathcal{R}\setminus\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny CS}}
``` |  |

where
$`y^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i}=\underset{1\leq k\leq K}{\operatorname{arg}\,\operatorname{max}}\;\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i,k}`$
and
$`y^{\text{\tiny GF}}_{i}=\underset{1\leq k\leq K}{\operatorname{arg}\,\operatorname{max}}\;\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GF}}_{i,k}`$
represent the predicted labels for $`v_{i}`$ by both pathways.
Intuitively, in the consensus set $`\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny CS}}`$,
both pathways produce the same label predictions, and thus, they can be
directly used as pseudo-labels, i.e.,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny CS}},\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GA}}=\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GA}}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny CS}},\text{and}\ \mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GF}}=\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GF}}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny CS}}.
``` |  |

As for the disagreement set $`\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}`$, we
further divide it into two subsets
$`\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GA}}`$ and
$`\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GF}}`$, where each node
$`v_{i}`$ in the former set has a higher confidence score
$`\omega^{\text{\tiny GA}}=\max_{1\leq k\leq K}\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i,k}`$
from the GA pathway compared to the GF one
($`\omega^{\text{\tiny GA}}=\max_{1\leq k\leq K}\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i,k}`$),
while the opposite is true for the latter. The pseudo-labels of the
nodes in $`\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GA}}`$ and
$`\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GF}}`$ are thus determined
by $`\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}}`$ and
$`\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GF}}`$, respectively. Accordingly, the labeled
node sets are expanded as follows:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GA}}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GF}},\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GA}}=\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GA}}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GA}},\ \text{and}\ \mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GF}}=\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GF}}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GF}}.
``` |  |

### 4.2. WSD-based Graph Sketching

After the obtainment of soft labels $`\mathbf{P}`$, the next step in
STAD is to construct a sparse sketching matrix
$`\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}`$ such that the sketches
of $`\mathbf{A}`$, $`\mathbf{X}`$, and label matrix of $`\mathcal{G}`$
can be used as the adjacency matrix
$`\mathbf{A}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{N^{\prime}\times N^{\prime}}`$,
attribute matrix
$`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{N^{\prime}\times D}`$, and label
matrix $`\mathbf{Y}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{N^{\prime}}`$ of the
condensed TAG $`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$, respectively. More precisely,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (6) |  |
``` math
\mathbf{A}^{\prime}=\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{S},\ \mathbf{X}^{\prime}=\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{X}.
``` |  |

and for each node $`v_{i}\in\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$, its synthetic label
is constructed as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (7) |  |
``` math
\mathbf{Y}^{\prime}_{i,k}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }k=\underset{1\leq k\leq K}{\operatorname{arg}\,\operatorname{max}}\;{(\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{P})}_{i,:}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}.
``` |  |

Akin to the count-sketch ([Clarkson and Woodruff, 2017](#bib.bib35)), we
impose a one-hot constraint over $`\mathbf{S}`$ for sparsity, wherein
each row in $`\mathbf{S}`$ contains a single non-zero entry indicating
the hashing or sampling of the node into a bucket.

Sketching Objective. Inspired by our empirical observations in
§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3. Preliminary Studies ‣ 3. Preliminaries ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation"),
a desired $`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$ obtained by
Eq. ([6](#S4.E6 "Equation 6 ‣ 4.2. WSD-based Graph Sketching ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation"))
should have small WSD distances from $`\mathcal{G}`$ in terms of textual
attributes and graph topology, leading to the following objectives:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (8) |  |
``` math
\min_{\mathbf{S}}{\textsf{WSD}(f(\mathbf{A}),f(\mathbf{A}^{\prime}))},\ \text{and}\ \min_{\mathbf{S}}{\textsf{WSD}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{X}^{\prime})},
``` |  |

where $`f(\cdot)`$ stands for an embedding function that maps
$`\mathbf{A}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}`$ and
$`\mathbf{A}^{\prime}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{N^{\prime}}`$ to vectors of the
same dimensions. Since
Fig. [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2. 2-Wasserstein Distance (WSD) ‣ 3. Preliminaries ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
shows that
$`\textsf{WSD}(\textsf{GNN}(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{X}),\textsf{GNN}(\mathbf{A}^{\prime},\mathbf{X}^{\prime}))`$
exhibits the same trends as that of the single modality, and
Fig. [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3.2. 2-Wasserstein Distance (WSD) ‣ 3. Preliminaries ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
uncovers that $`\textsf{GNN}(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{X})`$ fails to fully
capture the features in $`\textsf{MLP}(\mathbf{X})`$, we thus transform
Eq. ([8](#S4.E8 "Equation 8 ‣ 4.2. WSD-based Graph Sketching ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation"))
into the joint minimization of
$`\textsf{WSD}(\textsf{GNN}(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{X}),\textsf{GNN}(\mathbf{A}^{\prime},\mathbf{X}^{\prime}))`$
and
$`\textsf{WSD}(\textsf{MLP}(\mathbf{X}),\textsf{MLP}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime}))`$.

###### Lemma 4.1.

For any matrix $`\mathbf{M}`$, the minimization of
$`\textsf{{WSD}}(\mathbf{M},\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{M})`$ is equivalent
to
$`\min_{\mathbf{S}}{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N^{\prime}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{1}_{\mathbf{S}_{k,i}\neq 0}\cdot\left\|\mathbf{M}_{i}-\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{S}_{k,j}\mathbf{M}_{j}\right\|_{2}^{2}}`$.

Since $`\mathbf{S}`$ has a single non-zero entry per row, the sketching
matrix $`\mathbf{S}`$ can be represented as a set of disjoint clusters
$`\{\mathcal{C}_{1},\mathcal{C}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{N^{\prime}}\}`$
where $`\mathcal{C}_{k}=\{v_{i}\in\mathcal{V}|\ \mathbf{S}_{k,i}>0\}`$.
Accordingly, $`\mathbb{1}_{\mathbf{S}_{k,i}\neq 0}`$ can be seen as a
cluster indicator and
$`\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{S}_{k,j}\mathbf{M}_{j}=\sum_{v_{j}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}{\mathbf{S}_{k,j}\mathbf{M}_{j}}`$
can be perceived as the weighted centroid of the cluster
$`\mathcal{C}_{k}`$. The objective in
Lemma [4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma 4.1. ‣ 4.2. WSD-based Graph Sketching ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
can be rewritten as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\min_{\{\mathcal{C}_{1},\mathcal{C}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{N^{\prime}}\}}{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N^{\prime}}\sum_{v_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\left\|\mathbf{M}_{i}-\sum_{v_{j}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\mathbf{S}_{k,j}\mathbf{M}_{j}\right\|_{2}^{2}}.
``` |  |

In other words,
Lemma [4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma 4.1. ‣ 4.2. WSD-based Graph Sketching ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")¹¹
1 The proof can be found in Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Theoretical Proof ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
implies that the construction of sketching matrix $`\mathbf{S}`$ towards
optimizing our above WSD-based objective can be equivalently perceived
as the clustering over feature vectors
$`\textsf{GCN}(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{H}^{\text{\tiny GA}}`$ and
$`\textsf{MLP}(\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{H}^{\text{\tiny GF}}`$.

According to
Eq. ([4](#S4.E4 "Equation 4 ‣ 4.1. Graph-Text Collaborative Encoding ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")),
$`\mathbf{P}`$ adaptively combines $`\mathbf{H}^{\text{\tiny GA}}`$ and
$`\mathbf{H}^{\text{\tiny GF}}`$ via attention weights. As such, instead
of joint clustering over both features, we simply cluster vectors in
$`\mathbf{P}`$, leading to the following optimization objective for
deriving the sketching matrix $`\mathbf{S}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (9) |  |
``` math
\min_{\{\mathcal{C}_{1},\mathcal{C}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{N^{\prime}}\}}{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N^{\prime}}\sum_{v_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\left\|\mathbf{P}_{i}-\sum_{v_{j}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\mathbf{S}_{k,j}\mathbf{P}_{j}\right\|_{2}^{2}}.
``` |  |

Construction of $`\mathbf{S}`$. The objective function in
Eq. ([9](#S4.E9 "Equation 9 ‣ 4.2. WSD-based Graph Sketching ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation"))
is a within-cluster sum of squares, if we set the weight
$`\mathbf{S}_{k,j}`$ of each node $`v_{j}`$ to
$`\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}`$, which can be solved by the well-known
K-Means algorithm ([Lloyd, 1982](#bib.bib33)). However, the class labels
of nodes are obtained by hardmax discretization of softmax distributions
$`\mathbf{P}`$ or $`\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{P}`$ (see
Eq. ([7](#S4.E7 "Equation 7 ‣ 4.2. WSD-based Graph Sketching ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation"))).
The clustering of softmax distributions is likely to group nodes with
distinct labels into the same cluster. To alleviate this issue, we
additionally employ a greedy reassignment scheme as a post-refinement of
$`\mathbf{S}`$. More concretely, we first evaluate the affinity between
each class label $`y_{k}\in\mathcal{Y}`$ ($`1\leq k\leq K`$) and each
cluster
$`\mathcal{C}_{j}\in\{\mathcal{C}_{1},\mathcal{C}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{N^{\prime}}\}`$
by computing the fraction of the total population of label $`y_{k}`$
that falls into $`\mathcal{C}_{j}`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{|\{v_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{j}|\ \mathbf{Y}_{i,k}=1\}|}{|\{v_{i}\in\mathcal{V}|\ \mathbf{Y}_{i,k}=1\}|}.
``` |  |

We then pick, for each class, the class-cluster pair with the highest
affinity value, and then select the remaining class-cluster pairs with
the highest affinity values among all the $`K\times N^{\prime}`$ pairs
until obtaining top-$`N^{\prime}`$ pairs in total. The nodes in each of
these classes will be finally assigned to the corresponding cluster. For
each node $`v_{i}`$ without a final assignment in the above step, its
cluster is updated to the one whose centroid has the minimum distance to
$`v_{i}`$’s label distribution among the selected clusters of the same
predicted class.

### 4.3. Keywords-based Text Synthesis with LLMs

It is necessary to generate corresponding readable texts of each node in
$`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$, which can be utilized in downstream LLM-based
tasks and make it easier for human understanding. Notice that the sparse
sketching matrix $`\mathbf{S}`$ obtained in the preceding section
essentially partitions the nodes in $`\mathcal{G}`$ into disjoint
clusters
$`\{\mathcal{C}_{1},\mathcal{C}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{N^{\prime}}\}`$,
each of which corresponds to a node in $`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$.
Intuitively, the textual attributes of each node
$`v^{\prime}_{i}\in\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$ should be a summarization of
the text sequences of nodes in its corresponding cluster
$`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$. Traditional text distillation maps the synthetic
embeddings to discrete synthetic texts ([Morris et al.,
2023](#bib.bib48)) via vector to text (V2T), which may involve poor
cross-architecture generalization, high tuning overhead, and low
interpretability.

To address these limitations, we directly invoke an LLM to summarize the
original texts corresponding to nodes within each cluster, obtaining the
synthetic texts without intermediate embedding-to-text mapping. However,
directly processing clustered texts via LLMs is both highly
time-consuming and financially costly. To cost-effectively leverage the
massive knowledge and remarkable generative abilities of LLMs for the
summarization fulfilling the above goals, STAD resorts to a three-phase
approach.

Cluster-based Keyword Extraction. Instead of simply assembling all the
text sequences in each cluster $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$ as the input to LLMs,
which not only comprises substantial noisy and redundant information but
also entails a high query cost, our solution is to first sift out the
keywords from the text sequences
$`\mathcal{S}_{i}=\{s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{|\mathcal{C}_{i}|}\}`$ of each
cluster $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$. Towards this end, we define the
intra-cluster TF-IDF for each word $`w`$ as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (10) |  |
``` math
\text{TF-IDF}(w,\mathcal{S}_{i})=\text{TF}(w,\mathcal{S}_{i})\times\text{IDF}(w,\mathcal{S}_{i}),
``` |  |

where $`\text{TF}(w,\mathcal{S}_{i})`$ and
$`\text{IDF}(w,\mathcal{S}_{i})`$ are formulated by

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{gathered}\text{TF}(w,\mathcal{S}_{i})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{i}|}\sum_{k=1}^{|\mathcal{C}_{i}|}\frac{\#(w,s_{k})}{\underset{w^{\prime}\in s_{k}}{\max}\#(w^{\prime},s_{k})},\ \text{IDF}(w,\mathcal{S}_{i})=\log\left(\frac{|\mathcal{C}_{i}|}{1+\text{df}(w,\mathcal{S}_{i})}\right).\end{gathered}
``` |  |

Particularly, $`\#(w,s_{j})`$ is the frequency of word $`w`$ in text
$`s_{j}`$, and $`\text{df}(w,\mathcal{S}_{i})`$ denotes the number of
texts in $`\mathcal{S}_{i}`$ containing word $`w`$.

Accordingly, we next pick the top-$`2\xi`$ words with the highest
intra-cluster TF-IDF values in $`\mathcal{S}_{i}`$, followed by an
additional filtering step to prune the $`\xi`$ words with the smallest
Euclidean distances (SBERT embedding vectors) to the corresponding
attribute vector $`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{i}`$ of $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$.
Finally, we obtain a list of $`\xi`$ distinct words
$`\mathcal{W}_{i}=\{w_{i,1},w_{i,2},\dots,w_{i,\xi}\}`$ as the keywords
for cluster $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$ or condensed node $`v^{\prime}_{i}`$ in
$`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$. Notably, our keyword extraction jointly
considers words’ statistical importance (quantified by intra-cluster
TF-IDF) and semantic relevance (retained via embedding distance). Using
compact keywords instead of full sentences allows LLMs to capture more
entities within the same input length. Keywords as input can help with
interpretable text synthesis and enable flexible output by adjusting
keyword order or composition.

Candidate Text Generation with LLMs. Based on keywords
$`\mathcal{W}_{i}`$, we prompt an LLM to generate human-readable summary
text $`s^{\prime}_{i,j}`$ as a candidate text for
$`v^{\prime}_{i}\in\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (11) |  |
``` math
s^{\prime}_{i,j}=\textsf{LLM}(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{W}_{i},y^{\prime}_{i}),
``` |  |

where $`\mathcal{P}`$ signifies the prompt specifying the task
instruction and a formal description of $`\mathcal{G}`$’s domain, task,
and attribute characteristics, and $`y^{\prime}_{i}`$ is the semantic
label of $`v^{\prime}_{i}`$ derived in
Eq. ([6](#S4.E6 "Equation 6 ‣ 4.2. WSD-based Graph Sketching ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")).
In particular, STAD prompts the LLMs to generate a set of $`q`$
(typically $`q=3`$) candidate text
$`\{s^{\prime}_{i,1},s^{\prime}_{i,2},\dots,s^{\prime}_{i,q}\}`$ for
$`v^{\prime}_{i}`$.

WSD-Validation-guided Approximate Selection. Since each node in
$`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$ has $`q`$ candidate text sequences, it is still
prohibitively expensive to find the best synthetic textual attributes
due to the $`O(q^{N^{\prime}})`$ possible combinations. As a workaround,
STAD samples $`n_{s}`$ combinations of the candidate text for nodes in
$`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$ uniformly at random, yielding $`n_{s}`$
candidate graphs with distinct text sequences
$`\{s^{(j)\prime}_{1},s^{(j)\prime}_{2},\dots,s^{(j)\prime}_{N^{\prime}}\}_{j=1}^{n_{s}}`$.
Based thereon, each set of text sequences is converted into an attribute
matrix $`\mathbf{X}^{(j)\prime}`$ via a pre-trained text encoder (i.e.,
SBERT). We select the top-$`k`$ (often $`k=5`$) candidates with the
smallest WSD to $`\mathbf{X}`$, evaluate their downstream task
performance on the original dataset, and choose the one achieving the
highest validation accuracy as the final textual attributes for
$`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$.

## 5. Experiments

We conduct experiments to address the following questions. First, how
does the STAD perform on semi-supervised TAGD tasks? Second, how can
$`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$ generated by STAD help LL4TAG methods? Third,
how do the modules in STAD contribute to the overall performance?

### 5.1. Experimental Settings

Dataset. Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.3. Keywords-based Text Synthesis with LLMs ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
summarizes TAG datasets: citation networks Cora, Citeseer ([Yang et al.,
2016](#bib.bib2)), DBLP ([Ji et al., 2010](#bib.bib6)); E-commerce
co-view networks Computers, Photo, History ([Yan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib7)); and WikiCS ([Yan et al., 2023](#bib.bib7)) (Wikipedia
CS pages).

Baselines. We compare with the following recent baselines:

- •
  Graph distillation: GCond ([Jin et al., 2022](#bib.bib28)), GCDM ([Liu
  et al., 2022](#bib.bib40)), GDEM ([Liu et al., 2024](#bib.bib31)),
  ClustGDD ([Lai et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)), CGC ([Gao et al.,
  2025](#bib.bib43));
- •
  Text distillation: ASD ([Maekawa et al., 2023](#bib.bib38)),
  DaLLME ([Tao et al., 2024](#bib.bib45)). We also include
  topology-removed variants TCond, TCDM, ClustTDD (replacing
  $`\mathbf{A},\mathbf{A}^{\prime}`$ with identity matrices
  $`\mathbf{I},\mathbf{I}^{\prime}`$, respectively).

STAD has two variants: STAD($`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}`$) and
STAD($`\mathcal{S}^{\prime}`$). STAD($`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}`$) trains a
GCN on $`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}`$, $`\mathbf{A}^{\prime}`$,
$`\mathbf{Y}^{\prime}`$ and evaluates it on $`\mathbf{X}`$,
$`\mathbf{A}`$, $`\mathbf{Y}`$. For STAD($`\mathcal{S}^{\prime}`$),
$`\mathcal{S}^{\prime}`$ is remapped to
$`\mathbf{X}^{\prime\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{N^{\prime}\times D}`$ via
SBERT, then a GCN is trained on $`\mathbf{X}^{\prime\prime}`$,
$`\mathbf{A}^{\prime}`$, $`\mathbf{Y}^{\prime}`$ and evaluated on
$`\mathbf{X}`$, $`\mathbf{A}`$, $`\mathbf{Y}`$.

Implementation Details. We use five random splits with 20 nodes per
class (or all if fewer exist). GCN and MLP are two-layer (hidden 64, lr
0.01, weight decay $`0.0005`$). Text synthesis uses Qwen3-max (API);
LLM4TAG training/inference uses Qwen3-1.7B ([Yang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib52)).

### 5.2. Node Classification Performance Evaluation

Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3. Keywords-based Text Synthesis with LLMs ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
validates our design: WSD-guided dual-path encoding and keyword-based
text synthesis yield strong, stable compression. Graph distillation
generally outperforms text-only distillation, consistent with full
models (GCN vs. MLP). With $`r=0.05`$, GCond and GCDM fall below TCond
and TCDM, likely due to over-smoothing on low-quality synthetic
topology. Gradient-based methods (GCond, TCond) are unstable as $`r`$
decreases, e.g., GCond on Cora drops from 72.8%$`\pm`$2.0 to
45.8%$`\pm`$5.2. Clustering-based methods (ClustGDD, CGC, ClustTDD,
DaLLME) are more competitive and stable, and GDEM achieves good
performance via spectral alignment. STAD($`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}`$) and
STAD($`\mathcal{S}^{\prime}`$) achieve overall best accuracy. On WikiCS
at $`r{=}0.5`$, STAD($`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}`$) reaches 76.8%,
outperforming full GCN (75.9%) and the next-best distillation (71.4%).
STAD on distilled data sometimes exceeds full-data training, which we
attribute to effective extraction of discriminative information and
noise reduction. STAD($`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}`$) usually beats
STAD($`\mathcal{S}^{\prime}`$) because $`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}`$ preserves
semantics via direct aggregation; $`\mathbf{X}^{\prime\prime}`$ from
$`\mathcal{S}^{\prime}`$ incurs information loss from SBERT’s 256-token
limit. STAD($`\mathcal{S}^{\prime}`$) achieves relative better
performance on TAGs with large scale. This observation arises because
clusters with richer text provide more context and statistical evidence,
yielding more representative, informative keywords.

### 5.3. LLM4TAG Performance Evaluation

We train three LLM4TAG methods, GNN-LLM ([Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)),
ENGINE ([Zhu et al., 2024](#bib.bib18)), and TAPE ([He et al.,
2024](#bib.bib19)), with $`r=0.5`$. To ensure fair comparison, we use
V2T ([Morris et al., 2023](#bib.bib48)) to map synthetic attribute
matrices to text.
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.2. Node Classification Performance Evaluation ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
shows that STAD achieves the best transfer performance to these
frameworks. On Cora, STAD reaches 70.9%, 73.9%, and 70.4% on the three
methods, respectively, outperforming all baselines and narrowing the gap
to the full-data baseline. On History, STAD attains 76.6%, 74.6%, and
74.3%, surpassing the full-data baseline for ENGINE and TAPE.
Human-readable synthetic texts preserve the semantics required by
LLM4TAG models; in contrast, GCond and GDEM with V2T perform poorly,
likely due to embedding misalignment caused by V2T.

We also use STAD($`\mathcal{S}^{\prime}`$) for training-free LLM4TAG,
which includes two modes: Direct (i.e., LLMs directly give predictions
based on node texts) and Neighbor Summarization (NS, i.e., LLMs first
summarize the text of a node’s neighbors, then make predictions based on
the node’s own text and the neighbor summary). We apply
STAD($`\mathcal{S}^{\prime}`$) via in-context learning (ICL): prompts
are constructed based on the distances between input embeddings and
synthetic node attributes.
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.2. Node Classification Performance Evaluation ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
shows consistent performance gains: on Cora, we observe +2.4% (Direct)
and +3.6% (Nbr.Sum.); on History, the gains are +9.9% and +17.7%. These
results show that synthetic texts are effective ICL exemplars.

### 5.4. Ablation Study

We conduct ablation studies with $`r=0.05`$ to validate the
effectiveness of modules in our framework in
Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.4. Ablation Study ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation").
(w/o: module removing, w: another module as alternative.) Removing the
GA pathway leads to significant performance degradation, particularly on
Photo, where accuracy drops by 11.5%, indicating the critical role of
graph structure. Disabling CoST consistently reduces performance across
all datasets, confirming that it effectively enhances the dual-pathway
architecture. Removing our reassignment after K-Means hurts results,
validating the necessity of reassignment for more pure clusters. We omit
graph-text collaborative encoding and employ raw attributes from SBERT
for sketching. The performance decline verifies the necessity of the
encoding module. Furthermore, applying vanilla self-training to
dual-path encoders and baseline methods (e.g., GCDM+ST) yields inferior
performance compared to STAD($`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}`$), demonstrating the
superiority of Graph-Text Collaborative Encoding in semi-supervised
distillation. We evaluate alternative text generation strategies.
Variants without LLM summarization, with random words, or with key
sentences all underperform our keywords-based approach, with random
words causing severe degradation up to 15.5% on Photo. We build
summarization prompts without synthetic label injection, causing
performance drops and instability across most datasets. This proves that
synthetic label constraints enable LLMs to produce more category-aware
summaries. Direct generation without candidate set construction also
reduces accuracy, validating the importance of candidate selection.
Finally, we select candidates only via WSD. Results show both WSD scores
and validation accuracy are essential for optimal candidate selection.

### 5.5. Evaluation of LLMs for Text Synthesis

Table [6](#S5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 5.5. Evaluation of LLMs for Text Synthesis ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
compares LLM performance and cost for text synthesis  ²² 2
https://www.aliyun.com/, https://www.deepseek.com/, https://openai.com
with $`r=0.05`$. Qwen3-max achieves the best results on both datasets
(73.9% on Cora, 73.4% on History) at moderate cost, while smaller Qwen3
variants (1.7B–8B) offer competitive accuracy with significantly lower
expense. Scaling model size within the Qwen3 series does not
consistently improve performance, with 8B outperforming 32B on Cora.
GPT-5 achieve comparable accuracy to top performers but at 5–7$`\times`$
higher price. All methods yield similar low token usage, compared to the
full graphs³³ 3 Token number estimated by
https://pypi.org/project/tiktoken/. Overall, cost-efficient models match
or exceed expensive alternatives, suggesting model selection matters
more than scale for this task.

### 5.6. In-depth Analysis of CoST and Sketching

Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.6. In-depth Analysis of CoST and Sketching ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
tracks accuracy across CoST iterations, i.e., self-training steps with
progressively increasing pseudo-label ratio, for the GA and GF pathways,
and the fused final prediction. GA consistently outperforms GF while
final prediction exceeds both, and performance gaps narrow over
iterations as joint optimization on pseudo-labels enables bidirectional
knowledge transfer. All curves rise rapidly, then plateau or decline,
with optimal iterations varying across datasets. We thus iterate until
unlabeled nodes are exhausted and select the checkpoint with the highest
validation performance.

Here we define the overall purity of clusters in sketching as
$`\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{N^{\prime}}\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}|\{v_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{j}:y_{i}=y\}|}{N}`$,
which measures the extent to which clusters contain nodes of a single
class. As shown in
Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.6. In-depth Analysis of CoST and Sketching ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation"),
reassignment consistently improves purity,e.g., WikiCS exhibits the
largest relative improvement (from 0.64 to 0.79), indicating that
reassignment is effective for datasets with initially noisy cluster
structures. These results validate that our reassignment after
clustering successfully refines cluster quality, improving sketching.

### 5.7. Hyperparameter Analysis

Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.7. Hyperparameter Analysis ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
examines four key hyperparameters. Increasing input keywords $`\xi`$
from 64 to 512 improves Cora gradually to 74.5%, while History remains
stable around 73.3% and then drops to 70.6% at 512, suggesting excessive
keywords may introduce noise. Output tokens limits $`\kappa`$ show
similar divergence: Cora improves to 73.9% at $`\kappa=256`$ while
History at 73.4% with $`\kappa=12`$. For the number of candidate
summaries per cluster $`q`$. Our method is robust on Cora with
74.0$`\pm`$0.2% across $`q\in\{2,3,4,5\}`$. History drops to 70.4% at
$`q=4`$ but recovers at $`q=5`$; For number of candidate synthetic
graphs $`n_{s}`$,Cora maintains 72.8%–74.1% across
$`\{10,50,100,200\}`$. History improves from 72.9% to 75.5%,
demonstrating larger pools benefit complex textual datasets.

### 5.8. Visualization

As shown in
Figure [7](#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 5.8. Visualization ‣ 5. Experiments ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation"),
t-SNE visualizations of node attributes reveal that original data
features exhibit entangled class boundaries, while synthetic features
generated by our distillation method form clearly separated clusters.
This result confirms that our distillation strategy not only preserves
but also sharpens class-discriminative structural information, even with
substantial compression ratios.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 7. t-SNE of node attributes: original ($`\mathbf{X}`$) vs.
synthetic ($`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}`$) on Cora and History.

### 5.9. Conclusion

This paper proposes STAD for semi-supervised TAG distillation. Guided by
WSD, STAD introduces three modules: graph-text collaborative encoding,
WSD-based graph sketching, and keywords-based LLM text synthesis. STAD
achieves the state-of-the-art performance compared to current graph and
text distillation methods on various real-world datasets. The synthetic
TAGs obtained from STAD enable downstream LLM4Graph methods to be
efficient and effective. A potential direction for future work is to
explore multi-modal graph distillation for continual learning.

## Appendix A Complete Algorithm and Analysis

This section provides a formal algorithmic description of the STAD
framework along with a detailed complexity analysis of its three core
modules.

Algorithm Overview.
Algorithms [1](#algorithm1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix A Complete Algorithm and Analysis ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation"),
[2](#algorithm2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix A Complete Algorithm and Analysis ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation"),
and [3](#algorithm3 "Algorithm 3 ‣ Appendix A Complete Algorithm and Analysis ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
present the complete STAD pipeline, which takes a large-scale TAG
$`\mathcal{G}`$ as input and produces a compact synthetic TAG
$`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$ with human-readable text attributes.

Notation. We follow
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1. Notations and Problem Formulation ‣ 3. Preliminaries ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
for basic TAG notations: $`N=|\mathcal{V}|`$, $`M=|\mathcal{E}|`$, $`D`$
the feature dimension, $`K`$ the number of classes. For Module 1
(§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1. Graph-Text Collaborative Encoding ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")):
dual-pathway encoders GCN and MLP, hidden dimension $`h`$, attention
parameters $`\mathbf{W}_{\text{att}}\in\mathbb{R}^{h}`$ and
$`\mathbf{b}_{\text{att}}\in\mathbb{R}`$, soft labels
$`\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}}`$, $`\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GF}}`$,
$`\mathbf{P}`$, confidence scores
$`\max_{1\leq k\leq K}\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i,k}`$, pseudo-label
ratio $`\rho`$ with increment step $`0.1`$, consensus set
$`\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny CS}}`$ and disagreement subsets
$`\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GA}}`$,
$`\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GF}}`$, labeled sets
$`\mathcal{U}`$, $`\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GA}}`$,
$`\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GF}}`$. For Module 2
(§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2. WSD-based Graph Sketching ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")):
target condensed size $`N^{\prime}`$, sketching matrix
$`\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}`$, clusters
$`\{\mathcal{C}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{N^{\prime}}\}`$, K-Means
iterations. For Module 3
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3. Keywords-based Text Synthesis with LLMs ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")):
keyword count $`\xi`$, intra-cluster TF-IDF, keywords
$`\mathcal{W}_{i}`$, candidate count $`q`$ (typically $`q=3`$), prompt
$`\mathcal{P}`$, sample count $`n_{s}`$ (typically $`n_{s}=100`$),
top-$`k`$ validation (often $`k=5`$), text encoder (SBERT).

Input: TAG $`\mathcal{G}`$ with $`\mathbf{A}`$, $`\mathbf{X}`$,
$`\mathbf{Y}`$, and initial labeled set $`\mathcal{V}_{\text{tr}}`$.

Output: Soft labels $`\mathbf{P}`$ and labeled sets $`\mathcal{U}`$,
$`\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GA}}`$, $`\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GF}}`$.

1 Step 1 — Dual-pathway encoding.;

2
$`\mathbf{H}^{\text{\tiny GA}}\leftarrow\textsf{GCN}(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{X})`$;
$`\mathbf{H}^{\text{\tiny GF}}\leftarrow\textsf{MLP}(\mathbf{X})`$;

3
$`\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}}\leftarrow\textsf{softmax}(\mathbf{H}^{\text{\tiny GA}})`$;
$`\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GF}}\leftarrow\textsf{softmax}(\mathbf{H}^{\text{\tiny GF}})`$;

4 for *$`i=1`$ to $`N`$* do

    5
$`\alpha^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i}\leftarrow\sigma(\mathbf{W}_{\text{att}}\cdot\mathbf{H}_{i}^{\text{\tiny GA}}+\mathbf{b}_{\text{att}})`$;
$`\alpha^{\text{\tiny GF}}_{i}\leftarrow 1-\alpha^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i}`$;

    6
$`\mathbf{P}_{i}\leftarrow\textsf{softmax}(\alpha^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i}\odot\mathbf{H}_{i}^{\text{\tiny GA}}+\alpha^{\text{\tiny GF}}_{i}\odot\mathbf{H}_{i}^{\text{\tiny GF}})`$;

7 Step 2 — Collaborative self-training.;

8 Initialize $`\mathcal{U}\leftarrow\mathcal{V}_{\text{tr}}`$,
$`\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GA}}\leftarrow\mathcal{V}_{\text{tr}}`$,
$`\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GF}}\leftarrow\mathcal{V}_{\text{tr}}`$;
$`\rho\leftarrow 0.1`$;

9 while *$`\rho\leq 1.0`$* do

    10 Recompute $`\mathbf{H}^{\text{\tiny GA}}`$,
$`\mathbf{H}^{\text{\tiny GF}}`$, $`\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}}`$,
$`\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GF}}`$, $`\mathbf{P}`$;

    11 $`\mathcal{R}\leftarrow`$ top-$`\rho`$ proportion of unlabeled
nodes $`\mathcal{V}\setminus\mathcal{U}`$ by confidence
$`\max_{k}\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i,k}`$;

    12
$`\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny CS}}\leftarrow\{v_{i}\in\mathcal{R}\mid\underset{k}{\operatorname{arg}\,\operatorname{max}}\;\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i,k}=\underset{k}{\operatorname{arg}\,\operatorname{max}}\;\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GF}}_{i,k}\}`$;

    13
$`\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}\leftarrow\mathcal{R}\setminus\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny CS}}`$;

    14
$`\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GA}}\leftarrow\{v_{i}\in\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}\mid\max_{k}\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}}_{i,k}>\max_{k}\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GF}}_{i,k}\}`$;

    15
$`\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GF}}\leftarrow\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}\setminus\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GA}}`$;

    16
$`\mathcal{U}\leftarrow\mathcal{U}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny CS}}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GA}}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GF}}`$;

    17
$`\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GA}}\leftarrow\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GA}}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny CS}}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GA}}`$;

    18
$`\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GF}}\leftarrow\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GF}}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny CS}}\cup\mathcal{R}^{\text{\tiny DS}}_{\text{\tiny GF}}`$;

    19 Update $`\mathbf{W}_{\text{att}}`$, GCN, MLP by minimizing
$`\mathcal{L}=\textsf{CE}(\mathbf{P},\hat{\mathbf{Y}})+\textsf{CE}(\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GF}},\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\text{\tiny GF}})+\textsf{CE}(\mathbf{P}^{\text{\tiny GA}},\hat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\text{\tiny GA}})`$;

    20 $`\rho\leftarrow\rho+0.1`$;

21 return $`\mathbf{P}`$, $`\mathcal{U}`$,
$`\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GA}}`$, $`\mathcal{U}^{\text{\tiny GF}}`$;

Algorithm 1 Graph-Text Collaborative Encoding

Complexity Analysis. We analyze the time complexity of each module. Let
$`N`$ be the number of nodes, $`M`$ the number of edges, $`D`$ the
feature dimension of $`\mathbf{X}`$, $`L`$ the number of GCN layers,
$`h`$ the hidden dimension, $`K`$ the number of classes, $`T=10`$ the
number of self-training epochs ($`\rho`$ from $`0.1`$ to $`1.0`$ with
step $`0.1`$), $`I_{\text{km}}`$ the number of K-Means iterations, $`W`$
the average text length, $`V`$ the total vocabulary size (TF-IDF),
$`\mathcal{T}_{\text{LLM}}`$ the cost of one LLM call,
$`I_{\text{sink}}`$ the number of Sinkhorn iterations for WSD
computation, and $`C`$ the size of the sampled node subset used in WSD
($`N^{\prime}<C<N`$).

Module 1: Graph-Text Collaborative Encoding. The GA pathway (GCN with
$`L`$ layers) costs $`\mathcal{O}(L(MD+Nh^{2}))`$ for sparse matrix
multiplication and transformations. The GF pathway (MLP) costs
$`\mathcal{O}(NDh)`$. Attention fusion requires $`\mathcal{O}(Nh)`$.
Collaborative self-training repeats for $`T`$ iterations, each involving
confidence selection $`\mathcal{O}(N\log N)`$, consensus verification
$`\mathcal{O}(N)`$, and backpropagation $`\mathcal{O}(L(MD+Nh^{2}))`$.
Total for Module 1:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (12) |  |
``` math
\mathcal{T}_{\text{M1}}=\mathcal{O}(T\cdot L(MD+Nh^{2})+TN\log N)
``` |  |

Module 2: WSD-based Graph Sketching. K-Means clustering on $`N`$ soft
label vectors of dimension $`K`$ into $`N^{\prime}`$ clusters costs
$`\mathcal{O}(N\cdot N^{\prime}\cdot K\cdot I_{\text{km}})`$. Greedy
reassignment involves computing class-cluster affinities
$`\mathcal{O}(NK)`$ and distance computations
$`\mathcal{O}(NKN^{\prime})`$. Graph compression via sparse matrix
operations costs $`\mathcal{O}(ND+M+N^{\prime 2})`$. Total for Module 2:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (13) |  |
``` math
\mathcal{T}_{\text{M2}}=\mathcal{O}(NN^{\prime}K\cdot I_{\text{km}}+ND+M+N^{\prime 2})
``` |  |

Input: Soft labels $`\mathbf{P}`$, $`\mathbf{A}`$, $`\mathbf{X}`$,
$`\mathbf{Y}`$, and target size $`N^{\prime}`$.

Output: Sketching matrix $`\mathbf{S}`$ and condensed
$`\mathbf{A}^{\prime}`$, $`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}`$,
$`\mathbf{Y}^{\prime}`$.

1 Step 1 — $`K`$-Means clustering on soft labels.;

2
$`\{\mathcal{C}_{1},\mathcal{C}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{N^{\prime}}\}\leftarrow\textsf{K-Means}(\mathbf{P},N^{\prime})`$;

3 Construct $`\mathbf{S}`$ s.t.
$`\mathbf{S}_{k,i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}`$ if
$`v_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}`$, else $`0`$;

4 Step 2 — Greedy reassignment post-processing.;

5 for *$`k=1`$ to $`K`$* do

    6 for *$`j=1`$ to $`N^{\prime}`$* do

       7 Compute affinity
$`\frac{|\{v_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{j}|\ \mathbf{Y}_{i,k}=1\}|}{|\{v_{i}\in\mathcal{V}|\ \mathbf{Y}_{i,k}=1\}|}`$;

8 $`\{y_{k_{i}},\mathcal{C}_{k_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{N^{\prime}}\leftarrow`$ the
pairs with the highest affinity values;

9 Assign nodes with label $`y_{k_{i}}`$ to
$`\mathcal{C}_{k_{i}}\ \forall{1\leq i\leq N^{\prime}}`$;

10 for *each node $`v_{i}`$ w/o labels
$`\{y_{k_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{N^{\prime}}`$* do

    11 Add $`v_{i}`$ to $`\mathcal{C}_{k}`$ s.t.
$`\min_{1\leq k\leq N^{\prime}}\|\mathbf{P}_{i}-\textsf{Mean}(\mathcal{C}_{k})\|_{2}`$;

12 Update $`\mathbf{S}`$ accordingly;

13 Step 3 — Graph compression.;

14
$`\mathbf{A}^{\prime}\leftarrow\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{S}`$;
$`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}\leftarrow\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{X}`$;

15
$`\mathbf{Y}^{\prime}_{i,k}\leftarrow\begin{cases}1&\text{if }k=\underset{1\leq k^{\prime}\leq K}{\operatorname{arg}\,\operatorname{max}}\;{(\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{P})}_{i,k^{\prime}}\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}`$;

16 return $`\mathbf{S}`$, $`\mathbf{A}^{\prime}`$,
$`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}`$, $`\mathbf{Y}^{\prime}`$;

Algorithm 2 WSD-based Graph Sketching

Module 3: Keywords-based Text Synthesis. TF-IDF computation across
$`N^{\prime}`$ clusters with total vocabulary size $`V`$ costs
$`\mathcal{O}(VW\cdot N^{\prime}+N\cdot W)`$. SBERT-based keyword
filtering costs $`\mathcal{O}(N^{\prime}\xi D)`$. LLM generation for
$`N^{\prime}`$ nodes with $`q`$ candidates each costs
$`\mathcal{O}(N^{\prime}q\cdot\mathcal{T}_{\text{LLM}})`$. WSD
computation for $`n_{s}`$ candidate graphs using Sinkhorn algorithm
costs $`\mathcal{O}(n_{s}(N+N^{\prime})^{2}I_{\text{sink}})`$. In
practice, sampling a subset of original nodes with size $`C`$
($`N^{\prime}<C<N`$) is enough, so that the Sinkhorn algorithm can be
$`\mathcal{O}(n_{s}(C+N^{\prime})^{2}I_{\text{sink}})`$. Total for
Module 3:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (14) |  |
``` math
\mathcal{T}_{\text{M3}}=\mathcal{O}(VWN^{\prime}+N^{\prime}\xi D+N^{\prime}q\cdot\mathcal{T}_{\text{LLM}}+n_{s}(C+N^{\prime})^{2}I_{\text{sink}})
``` |  |

Overall Complexity. The total time complexity is
$`\mathcal{T}_{\texttt{STAD}{}}=\mathcal{T}_{\text{M1}}+\mathcal{T}_{\text{M2}}+\mathcal{T}_{\text{M3}}`$.
The space complexity is dominated by storing the adjacency matrix
($`\mathcal{O}(M)`$), feature matrices
($`\mathcal{O}(ND+N^{\prime}h)`$), soft labels ($`\mathcal{O}(NK)`$),
and candidate texts ($`\mathcal{O}(N^{\prime}qW)`$), yielding
$`\mathcal{S}_{\texttt{STAD}{}}=\mathcal{O}(M+ND+N^{\prime}h+NK+N^{\prime}qW)`$.

In practice, since $`N^{\prime}\ll N`$, Module 3 operates efficiently
despite LLM calls. The dominant cost in Module 1 is the GCN operations
scaling linearly with edges $`M`$. Module 2’s clustering is efficient
when $`N^{\prime}`$ is small. The WSD validation in Module 3 uses a
small $`n_{s}`$ (e.g., $`100`$) to balance quality and cost.

Input: Sketching matrix $`\mathbf{S}`$, clusters
$`\{\mathcal{C}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{N^{\prime}}\}`$, text
$`\mathcal{S}`$, labels $`\mathbf{Y}^{\prime}`$, integers $`\xi`$,
$`q`$, $`n_{s}`$, $`k`$, and prompt $`\mathcal{P}`$.

Output: Synthetic texts
$`\mathcal{S}^{\prime}=\{s^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,s^{\prime}_{N^{\prime}}\}`$
for $`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$.

1 Step 1 — Cluster-based keyword extraction.;

2 for *$`i=1`$ to $`N^{\prime}`$* do

    3
$`\mathcal{S}_{i}\leftarrow\{s_{j}\mid v_{j}\in\mathcal{C}_{i}\}`$;

    4
$`\text{TF-IDF}(w,\mathcal{S}_{i})=\text{TF}(w,\mathcal{S}_{i})\times\text{IDF}(w,\mathcal{S}_{i})`$
$`\forall{w\in\mathcal{S}_{i}}`$;

    5 Select top-$`2\xi`$ words by intra-cluster TF-IDF;

    6 Prune $`\xi`$ words with lowest embedding distance to
$`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{i}`$;

    7 Obtain keywords $`\mathcal{W}_{i}=\{w_{i,1},\ldots,w_{i,\xi}\}`$;

8 Step 2 — Candidate text generation with LLMs.;

9 for *$`i=1`$ to $`N^{\prime}`$* do

    10
$`y^{\prime}_{i}\leftarrow\underset{k}{\operatorname{arg}\,\operatorname{max}}\;\mathbf{Y}^{\prime}_{i,k}`$;

    11
$`\{s^{\prime}_{i,1},\ldots,s^{\prime}_{i,q}\}\leftarrow\textsf{LLM}(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{W}_{i},y^{\prime}_{i})`$;

12 Step 3 — WSD-validation-guided selection.;

13 for *$`l=1`$ to $`n_{s}`$* do

    14
$`\mathcal{S}^{\prime}_{l}\leftarrow\{s^{\prime}_{i,j_{i}}\mid i\in[N^{\prime}],j_{i}\sim\text{Uniform}([q])\}`$;

    15
$`\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{l}\leftarrow\text{SBERT}(\mathcal{S}^{\prime}_{l})`$;

    16 Compute
$`\text{WSD}_{l}\leftarrow\textsf{WSD}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{l})`$;

17 Select top-$`k`$ candidates with the lowest WSD;

18 Choose $`\mathcal{S}^{\prime}`$ with the best downstream task
performance;

19 return $`\mathcal{S}^{\prime}`$;

Algorithm 3 Keywords-based Text Synthesis with LLMs

## Appendix B Theoretical Proof

###### Proof of Lemma [4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma 4.1. ‣ 4.2. WSD-based Graph Sketching ‣ 4. Methodology ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation").

We establish this equivalence through the geometric form of the
2-Wasserstein distance in the context of graph sketching.

Step 1: Distribution construction. Let
$`\mathcal{P}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{\mathbf{M}_{i}}`$ denote
the empirical distribution of the original features, where
$`\delta_{\mathbf{M}_{i}}`$ is the Dirac delta distribution centered at
$`\mathbf{M}_{i}`$. The sketching matrix
$`\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}`$ induces a hard
clustering partition $`\{\mathcal{C}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{N^{\prime}}`$ of the
node set $`[N]`$, where
$`\mathcal{C}_{k}=\{i\in[N]:\mathbf{S}_{k,i}\neq 0\}`$ represents the
set of nodes assigned to the $`k`$-th condensed node.

By construction of $`\mathbf{S}`$ in
Algorithm [2](#algorithm2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix A Complete Algorithm and Analysis ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation"),
each row $`k`$ satisfies
$`\mathbf{S}_{k,i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}`$ if
$`i\in\mathcal{C}_{k}`$, and $`\mathbf{S}_{k,i}=0`$ otherwise.
Consequently, the compressed empirical distribution is
$`\mathcal{Q}=\sum_{k=1}^{N^{\prime}}\frac{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}{N}\delta_{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}}`$,
where the centroid
$`\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{S}_{k,j}\mathbf{M}_{j}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\mathbf{M}_{j}`$.

Step 2: Voronoi property verification. We verify that the partition
$`\{\mathcal{C}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{N^{\prime}}`$ satisfies the Voronoi
property under the squared Euclidean metric. For any sample
$`\mathbf{M}_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}`$ and any other cluster
$`k^{\prime}\neq k`$, the K-Means clustering in
Algorithm [2](#algorithm2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix A Complete Algorithm and Analysis ‣ Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation")
(Step 1) assigns each node to the nearest centroid, ensuring:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\|\mathbf{M}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|\mathbf{M}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k^{\prime}}\|_{2}^{2}.
``` |  |

Step 3: Optimal transport plan. Consider the transport plan
$`\gamma^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}`$ induced by the
clustering:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\gamma^{*}_{ik}=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{N},&\text{if }\mathbf{M}_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{k},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
``` |  |

This plan is feasible: (i)
$`\sum_{k=1}^{N^{\prime}}\gamma^{*}_{ik}=\frac{1}{N}`$ for all $`i`$
(marginal of $`\mathcal{P}`$), and (ii)
$`\sum_{i=1}^{N}\gamma^{*}_{ik}=\frac{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}{N}`$ for all
$`k`$ (marginal of $`\mathcal{Q}`$).

Step 4: Optimality via Voronoi property. For any feasible transport plan
$`\gamma`$, the Voronoi property yields the pointwise lower bound for
each $`i`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\sum_{k=1}^{N^{\prime}}\gamma_{ik}\|\mathbf{M}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}\geq\sum_{k=1}^{N^{\prime}}\gamma_{ik}\|\mathbf{M}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k(i)}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{N}\|\mathbf{M}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k(i)}\|_{2}^{2},
``` |  |

where $`k(i)`$ denotes the cluster index of $`\mathbf{M}_{i}`$. Summing
over all $`i`$ gives:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N^{\prime}}\gamma_{ik}\|\mathbf{M}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}\geq\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|\mathbf{M}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k(i)}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N^{\prime}}\gamma^{*}_{ik}\|\mathbf{M}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}.
``` |  |

Thus $`\gamma^{*}`$ is optimal, and the squared WSD equals:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\textsf{WSD}^{2}(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{Q})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N^{\prime}}\sum_{\mathbf{M}_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\|\mathbf{M}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}\|_{2}^{2}.
``` |  |

Step 5: Equivalence to sketching objective. Rewriting using
$`\mathbb{1}_{[\mathbf{S}_{k,i}\neq 0]}=\mathbb{1}_{[i\in\mathcal{C}_{k}]}`$
and substituting
$`\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{S}_{k,j}\mathbf{M}_{j}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\textsf{WSD}^{2}(\mathbf{M},\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{M})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N^{\prime}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{1}_{[\mathbf{S}_{k,i}\neq 0]}\cdot\left\|\mathbf{M}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}\right\|_{2}^{2}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N^{\prime}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{1}_{[\mathbf{S}_{k,i}\neq 0]}\cdot\left\|\mathbf{M}_{i}-\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{S}_{k,j}\mathbf{M}_{j}\right\|_{2}^{2}.`$ |  |

Therefore, minimizing
$`\textsf{WSD}(\mathbf{M},\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{M})`$ is equivalent
to the stated minimization problem, which corresponds precisely to the
K-Means clustering objective in the feature space. ∎

## Appendix C TAG Distillation Time and LLM4TAG training Time

### C.1. TAG Distillation Time Comparison

Here we give a simple comparison between STAD and ClustGDD in terms of
distillation time, another efficient graph distillation method, at
$`r=0.05`$ on Cora and History. We select ClustGDD as the baseline
because it achieves both high efficiency and accuracy, being orders of
magnitude faster than other gradient-based or distribution-matching
distillation methods while maintaining competitive performance.

Experimental results demonstrate the efficiency trade-offs of the STAD
method: when utilizing an LLM for text synthesis in
$`\texttt{STAD}{}(\mathcal{S}^{\prime})`$, it consumes $`191.67`$
seconds and $`291.24`$ seconds on Cora and History datasets
respectively, which is slower than
$`\texttt{STAD}{}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime})`$. This overhead primarily stems
from calling the LLM to generate $`\mathcal{S}^{\prime}`$, which incurs
high computational complexity. Meanwhile, both variants lag far behind
ClustGDD ($`6.79`$ seconds and $`10.31`$ seconds). However, STAD
achieves higher accuracy and better interpretability than ClustGDD, as
demonstrated in previous experiments. Therefore, a time gap of the same
order of magnitude or even one order of magnitude larger is acceptable.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| Dataset | $`\texttt{STAD}{}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime})`$ | $`\texttt{STAD}{}(\mathcal{S}^{\prime})`$ | ClustGDD |
| Cora | 56.0 | 191.7 | 6.79 |
| History | 83.1 | 291.2 | 10.31 |

### C.2. Time Cost of LLM4TAG Methods on $`\mathcal{G}`$ and $`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$

We compare the preprocessing and training times (in seconds) of three
LLM4TAG methods,GNN-LLM ([Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)), ENGINE ([Zhu et
al., 2024](#bib.bib18)), and TAPE ([He et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)) on the
original graph $`\mathcal{G}`$ and the distilled graph
$`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$ at distillation ratio $`r=0.5`$. GNN-LLM
extracts LLM last-layer representation to train GNNs; ENGINE fuses
intermediate-layer LLM representations for GNN training; TAPE prompts
LLMs to generate predictions and natural language explanations for
textual graph data, incurring substantially higher computational costs
due to autoregressive generation.

Preprocessing Time Analysis. The preprocessing time is substantially
reduced on the distilled graph $`\mathcal{G}^{\prime}`$ compared to the
original graph $`\mathcal{G}`$ for all three methods. The reduction is
most pronounced for TAPE, which requires invoking LLMs to generate
predictions and explanations for each node. On Cora, TAPE’s
preprocessing time drops from 2,784.7s to 50.0s (55.7$`\times`$
speedup); on the larger History dataset, it decreases from 32,756.0s to
75.0s (436.7$`\times`$ speedup). This dramatic improvement stems from
STAD reducing the graph size, thereby minimizing the number of expensive
LLM API calls. GNN-LLM and ENGINE also benefit from distillation, though
with more modest reductions, as they only require forward passes through
the LLM to obtain embeddings or intermediate representations, avoiding
the costly autoregressive generation process. Due to the early stopping,
GNN-LLM spends less time on the larger dataset History.

For GNN-LLM and TAPE, training times remain similar between

training is already efficient even on the full graph. ENGINE shows a
more noticeable reduction on History (from 121.3s to 86.4s), likely due
to its architecture-specific fusion mechanism benefiting from the
smaller distilled graph.
````
